ce_cne_land_reform_reason.value: This movement began with the Western Qin Great Revolution of 1810. People of the age understood it as a modern economic transformation arising among the agrarian states of the East, where powerful lineages had long dominated rural life. Through purchase or compulsory confiscation, land accumulated beyond all measure by its old owners was redistributed among a portion of the peasantry. The aim was to break the lineages’ hold over the rural population. The ruling group of the Empire of China suspended the movement during its rise to power. Around Mu Zhongtang’s southern campaign of 1820, however, he and his confidants revived it to restore the economy, free productive activity and mobilise peasants and soldiers.

flavorCNE.3.d.value:
Our revised laws on land, employment and family relations have reached every corner of the Empire and established a new economic order. We have freed people from the bonds of kinship that held them for thousands of years. The fields have returned to their proper place as a natural resource.

As the old lineages and their land can no longer bind the peasantry, young faces, dusty yet full of life, stream from the countryside into the cities. They dream of a new life built through human intelligence and science. The remnants of hereditary power disguise themselves as local associations and try to regain control over them. Police batons and the magistrate’s gavel will break their ambitions.

Once more we have brought the founding emperor Mu Zhongtang’s ideals into reality. We have shown that this Empire was built for the interests of the Huaxia nation. It will protect even the weakest person’s freedom to choose a future. Those now seeking happiness in the cities are bringing new prosperity to the Empire.

flavorCNE.6.d.value: Land commissioners in [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_mess_imprisonment_state').GetName] have arrested villagers who drafted petitions over disputed titles and placed them in military custody for concealing property. Officers widened the arrests to local gentry, teachers and clerks who kept the old deeds.\n\nThe new law empowers officials to settle land ownership, but also permits farmers to defend their property. A prosecution would make the reform's own agents answer for crimes committed in its name.

flavorCNE.8.d.value: The streets of [SCOPE.sState('cne_land_reform_peasants_in_city_state').GetName] are filling with newcomers from the countryside. Farming families have sold their land and come in search of wages. Employment brokers send them to factories and building sites, deducting recruitment and lodging charges from their pay.\n\nWorkers have accused the brokers of withholding contracts and enforcing old debts. In these growing towns, the promise that peasants could leave their old estates and freely earn a living faces its first practical tests.

flavorUSM.4.t.value: The Ming–Wu Succession: Zheng Zhao’s Audience
The Ming–Wu Succession: Zheng Zhao’s Audience

flavorUSM.4.d.value:
In the spring of 1678, Zheng Zhao—later Emperor Wuzong of Wu, then Duke of Wu, Ming’s Nanjing Protector and Minister of Rites—announced that he would visit the emperor after a succession of victories at home and overseas. The ruler of Yan at Tianjin, victorious in the Great Constitutional War thirty years earlier, still stood at the height of his power. Yet Zheng’s determination overcame his ministers’ warnings and his enemies’ threats. He set out in June.

Nothing comparable to this procession had been seen in the nearly three centuries of Northern Ming’s military governors and princely states. Pressure from Yan, Qin and Qi limited Zheng to five thousand guards and a handful of officials, but the entourage included the finest of Wu’s forces: marines from the Southern Seas, Japanese swordsmen, early Jurchen grenadiers, and even exiled nobles of the Far Eastern Yin seeking imperial redress and military aid. They carried treasures gathered during a century of Wu expansion across the world, while nearly ten thousand labourers hauled tribute rice from Annam and Cambodia. Beyond the procession lay a Central Plain kept close to famine by local fighting and the exactions of military governors and transport officials.

After returning, Zheng Zhao adopted the title of Supreme Lord. Wu and its colonies entered a period of rapid growth as refugees arrived from both north and south. Zheng and his successors pressed their centralising reforms and the commercialisation of land ever harder, securing the foundations of our authority over the Southern realm and its many states. Wu’s advance has continued to this day...

nesnd_hus_registration.1.d.value: The American civil war has unsettled the West, where Indigenous Americans have established a new khanate. Indigenous communities from both republics are moving there. Its new borders and claims to the land threaten to draw both republics into conflict.

[SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_khanate').GetName] has received four connected states on the American Great Plains. Half of the Indigenous populations remaining in the two source countries have joined it after cession. The new khan inherits the memory of an earlier uprising and faces intervention against the new order.

Monthly change: #v [Country.MakeScope.ScriptValue('nesnd_south_monthly_pressure_value')|1]#!. Pressure rises by #n +3#! each month, or #n +2.5#! under the Constitutional Settlement. Active reconciliation reduces it by #p 3#!.

#bold The First Minister's Case#!
From #v July 1837#!, the case may begin when pressure exceeds #v 24#!. From the beginning of #v 1838#!, an unresolved case involving Chen Dongyang, if he remains in the country, leads to the assassination and protection events. His death adds #n +25#! pressure, injury #n +10#!, and escape #n +3#!.

After the case is resolved, #v 70#! pressure permits an early accession. At #v 100#!, succession proceeds if Zheng Qin has departed. From the beginning of #v 1839#!, an unresolved dynastic dispute rises to #v 100#! once the First Minister's case has concluded. Succession and the other states' responses then proceed whether or not Zheng Qin is still alive. A peaceful settlement ends the dispute.

nesnd_south_succession_board_reason.value: Whose realm is Southern Ming: the Zhu emperor’s, or the Zheng family’s creation? Nanjing retains the imperial succession, while the Southern Administration in Hangzhou commands the troops and revenues that sustain reform. The Western provinces and Hangzhou could postpone their dispute over sovereign and minister while resisting the North. With reform reaching deep into provincial life, they can no longer avoid the question of who will govern.\n\nHuguang’s academies and Xiangfan’s troops uphold the Zhu succession, while Sichuan’s republicans continue to debate the Southern Administration’s reforms. Governors in the Southern Seas and lords in Japan weigh the land, money and soldiers a new dynasty might demand. Representatives in the Assembly of Rites, ministers in the cabinet and provincial commanders will eventually have to answer for their choices.
